speaking.text: Whistled languages exist wherever people needed to communicate across valleys too wide for shouting. They are not codes but full versions of the spoken language, with the pitch and rhythm of speech carried by a whistle that travels several kilometres. Speakers report understanding them as language rather than decoding them as signals.

Slime moulds have no nervous system and nonetheless solve problems that resemble planning. Placed in a maze with food at two exits, the organism withdraws from dead ends and leaves a connection along the shortest route. The behaviour emerges from simple local rules operating everywhere at once, with nothing coordinating them.

Guano was among the most valuable commodities of the nineteenth century, and the deposits accumulated over millennia were exhausted within about forty years. Nations went to war over islands consisting of little else, and the trade collapsed only when synthetic nitrogen fixation made the substance unnecessary.

Buildings designed to survive earthquakes are not built to be rigid. A structure that resists shaking absolutely must be immensely strong, whereas one designed to sway absorbs the energy and returns. Some modern towers rest on bearings that allow the ground to move beneath them while the building above stays comparatively still.

Before refrigeration, ice was cut from frozen lakes in winter, packed in sawdust, and shipped to tropical ports where it arrived largely intact. The trade seemed absurd to contemporaries and was extremely profitable, and it created an expectation of cold drinks that mechanical refrigeration was later invented to satisfy.

The safety razor was sold cheaply so that blades could be sold repeatedly, and the model has been imitated ever since. What is bought is not the object but access to a supply of consumables, and the profit sits entirely in the part that must be replaced rather than in the part that is kept.

chart.title: Cost per unit of three technologies, index where 2010 equals 100
chart.summary: All three fall but at very different rates. Solar modules drop to 11 per cent of their 2010 cost, an 89 per cent decline, with the steepest fall in the first three years. Battery cells follow a similar curve to 13. Offshore wind falls far less, to 46, roughly halving rather than collapsing. A strong answer notes that solar and batteries follow near-identical trajectories while wind is a different case, and that the steepest declines occur early and then flatten for all three.

chart.title: Four proposed high-speed rail routes
chart.summary: Cost does not track length. The Coastal route is the shortest of the three long options at 185 km yet costs 21.5 billion, nearly as much as the 310 km Northern link at 28. The Airport spur is only 42 km and saves just twelve minutes, but forecasts 11.7 million users a year, second highest. Cross-border is longest and dearest but forecasts fewer users than the spur. A strong answer states that neither length nor time saved predicts ridership, and identifies the Airport spur as the outlier on cost per passenger.

chart.title: Stages in producing a woven woollen cloth
chart.summary: Six stages from shearing to finishing. Scouring precedes carding because grease prevents fibres separating cleanly, and fulling comes last, deliberately shrinking and matting the woven cloth to make it dense and weather-resistant. A strong answer follows the order with connecting language, explains why scouring must precede carding, and notes that the final stage alters the fabric rather than merely tidying it.

lecture.transcript: I want to talk about queues, because almost every intuition people have about them is wrong, and the mathematics is genuinely surprising. Start with the central result. If arrivals at a service point are random rather than scheduled, the average waiting time does not rise gently as the system gets busier. It rises slowly up to about eighty per cent utilisation and then climbs almost vertically. At ninety-five per cent capacity, the average wait is roughly ten times what it was at fifty per cent, for the same service. This is why a hospital emergency department running at ninety-eight per cent occupancy is not slightly worse than one at eighty; it is in a completely different regime, and adding a small amount of capacity produces an enormous improvement. Now, the second counter-intuitive result concerns queue design. A single line feeding several servers is substantially better than separate lines for each server, even though the total staffing is identical. The reason is that separate lines allow one queue to stall behind a slow transaction while another server stands idle, and idle capacity in a congested system is pure waste. Banks and airports worked this out decades ago; supermarkets have mostly not, because customers dislike the appearance of a single long line even when it moves faster. And that is the third point, which is about perception rather than mathematics. Perceived waiting time depends heavily on whether the wait is occupied, whether it is explained, and whether people believe it is fair. An unexplained five-minute wait feels longer than an explained ten-minute one, and a queue that someone jumps generates complaints out of all proportion to the seconds lost.
key: with random arrivals, waiting time climbs almost vertically above about eighty per cent utilisation
at ninety-five per cent capacity the average wait is roughly ten times that at fifty per cent
small capacity additions produce enormous improvements in a congested system
a single line feeding several servers beats separate lines with identical staffing, because idle servers are pure waste
supermarkets resist this because customers dislike the look of one long line
perceived wait depends on occupation, explanation and fairness rather than duration alone

lecture.transcript: Today I want to trace how colour photography arrived, because the delay tells you something about what a technical problem actually consists of. Black and white photography was practical by the eighteen forties. Colour did not become ordinary until the nineteen sixties, and the gap of well over a century was not caused by anyone failing to have the idea. Maxwell demonstrated the principle in 1861: photograph the same scene three times through red, green and blue filters, then project the three images through the same filters superimposed, and the eye reconstructs the colour. It worked, and it was useless for practical purposes, because it required three exposures, three plates and a projection apparatus. Every subsequent approach was an attempt to compress that into one operation. The Lumière brothers coated a plate with dyed potato starch grains acting as millions of tiny filters, which was ingenious, produced beautiful results, and was slow and could not be reprinted. What eventually solved it was not optics at all but chemistry: a film carrying three separate light-sensitive layers stacked on top of one another, each sensitive to a different part of the spectrum, with the dyes formed during development. That required synthesising compounds that would stay in their own layer and not wander during processing, and the wandering problem took roughly thirty years to solve. So the obstacle was never the principle. It was a materials problem disguised as an imaging problem, and I would suggest that this is more common in the history of technology than the tidy narratives allow.
key: black and white was practical by the 1840s but colour only became ordinary in the 1960s
Maxwell demonstrated the three-filter principle in 1861, requiring three exposures and a projector
later approaches tried to compress this into one operation, such as the Lumière dyed starch plate
the eventual solution was a film with three stacked light-sensitive layers and dyes formed in development
the hard part was preventing dyes wandering between layers, which took about thirty years
the obstacle was a materials problem disguised as an imaging one

swt.passage: Counting a population is treated as an administrative task and is in fact a series of contested judgements, each with consequences for who receives money and representation. The first difficulty is definitional: a census must decide who counts as resident, and every answer excludes somebody. Students are counted in one place and pay for services in another; people with no fixed address may be counted nowhere; those working abroad for part of the year fall into a category that different countries resolve differently. The second difficulty is that the people hardest to count are not randomly distributed. Undercount concentrates among renters, recent migrants, young men and households where nobody wishes to be visible to a government agency, and it is therefore geographically concentrated too. Since census figures determine funding allocations and electoral boundaries, a systematic undercount transfers resources away from precisely the districts that were undercounted. Statistical adjustment can correct the aggregate reasonably well, and its use has been litigated repeatedly, because a method that changes which districts receive money is never merely technical. Several countries have abandoned the traditional door-to-door census in favour of combining existing administrative registers, which is cheaper and more current, and which relocates rather than removes the question of who the state has recorded.
key: defining residence is contested and every definition excludes somebody
students, homeless people and seasonal workers abroad are resolved differently between countries

swt.passage: Open access publishing was intended to remove the paywall between publicly funded research and the public that funded it, and in its dominant form it has relocated the barrier rather than removing it. Under the arrangement that has become standard, the reader pays nothing and the author's institution pays a processing charge, frequently several thousand pounds per article. For a well-funded laboratory this is an accounting matter. For a researcher in a low-income country, an independent scholar, or a discipline where grants are small and rare, it is a barrier of exactly the kind the movement set out to abolish, differing only in which end of the transaction it sits at. Waiver schemes exist and are applied inconsistently, and applying for one requires declaring poverty to the organisation deciding whether to publish you. Alternatives have been proposed and several work well in practice: institutional repositories, journals funded directly by consortia of libraries, and platforms that charge nothing at either end. None has displaced the processing charge model, and the reason is not technical. Prestige remains concentrated in established titles, hiring committees continue to read the journal name before the article, and no individual researcher can afford to publish where the assessment system does not look.
key: open access aimed to remove the reader paywall but relocated the barrier to authors
processing charges of several thousand pounds exclude poorly funded researchers and disciplines
waiver schemes are inconsistent and require declaring poverty to the publisher
working alternatives exist: repositories, library consortia funding and no-fee platforms
none has displaced the charge model because prestige remains with established titles

reading.passage: The distinction between a shortage of housing and a shortage of affordable housing is treated in public debate as a matter of emphasis, and it identifies two problems with different remedies. If the constraint is physical supply, then anything that increases the number of dwellings helps, including construction at the expensive end, since households moving into new stock vacate cheaper stock behind them. Evidence for this chain of moves is reasonably good in cities where it has been traced. If instead the constraint is that incomes at the lower end have fallen too far below any price at which building is profitable, additional market construction cannot reach those households at all, and the necessary instruments are subsidy, direct public building or income support. Most cities have both problems simultaneously and in different proportions, which is why the same policy produces contradictory results in different places. The debate becomes unproductive when each side generalises from a city where its own diagnosis happened to be correct, and neither position is unreasonable as a description of somewhere.

reading.passage: There is a widespread belief that creativity requires solitude, supported by a long tradition of describing the artist or scientist alone with a problem. Studies of how creative work is actually produced find a more particular pattern. The generation of unusual ideas does benefit from working alone, and group brainstorming reliably produces fewer distinct ideas than the same people thinking separately and pooling afterwards, largely because a group converges on the first plausible direction and because only one person can speak at a time. What groups do well is selection: judging which of a set of ideas is worth pursuing, a task at which individuals are markedly poorer because they are attached to their own. The practical conclusion is not that collaboration is overrated but that generation and evaluation are different activities, and the common practice of combining them in a single meeting does each of them badly.
reading.q: What does the passage conclude about creative work?
options: Idea generation is better done alone and evaluation better done in groups, so combining them in one meeting harms both.
Solitude is necessary for every stage of creative work.
Group brainstorming reliably produces more distinct ideas than individuals working separately.
Individuals are better than groups at judging which ideas are worth pursuing.

reading.passage: The phrase 'correlation is not causation' is repeated so frequently that it has begun to do harm, because it is now used to dismiss evidence rather than to interrogate it. The statement is true and nearly empty on its own. What matters is which of the alternative explanations for a correlation can be ruled out in a particular case: reverse causation, a common cause, or selection into the sample. Epidemiology established that smoking causes lung cancer without any randomised trial, by systematically eliminating these alternatives across dozens of studies with different designs and different populations, each vulnerable to a different bias. A criticism that merely names the maxim contributes nothing; a criticism that specifies which alternative explanation survives, and why, contributes a great deal. The distinction separates scepticism from its imitation.
reading.q: What is the author's main point?
options: Invoking the maxim is only useful when it names a specific alternative explanation that survives.
Correlational evidence should never be used to support causal claims.
Randomised trials are the only acceptable basis for establishing causation.
The link between smoking and lung cancer was established by randomised trials.

listening.transcript: I want to talk about why weather forecasting has a hard limit that no improvement in computing will remove. The story starts with Edward Lorenz in 1961, who was running a simple numerical weather model on an early computer. Wanting to repeat a run, he restarted it from the middle, typing in the numbers from a printout. The printout showed three decimal places while the machine held six, so the value he entered differed from the original by less than one part in a thousand. He expected a nearly identical result. What he got diverged completely within a simulated month or two. This was not a bug. It is a property of the equations. Systems of this kind amplify small differences exponentially, so that an error of any size, however tiny, grows until it dominates the forecast. Lorenz later illustrated it with the image of a butterfly, and the image has done some damage, because people take it to mean that the butterfly causes the storm. That is not the claim. The claim is that we cannot know the initial state of the atmosphere precisely enough, and that any imprecision, from any source, expands at a rate that sets a horizon of roughly two weeks. Now, the practical response has been interesting. Rather than pursuing a single forecast, meteorologists run the model dozens of times from slightly different starting conditions and look at the spread of results. If all fifty runs agree, confidence is high. If they scatter, it is low, and crucially the scatter itself is information about how predictable the situation is. So the discipline stopped trying to defeat the limit and started measuring it, which turned an insurmountable obstacle into a quantity that could be reported.
key: Lorenz restarted a model with values rounded to three decimal places instead of six
the results diverged completely within a simulated month or two, and this was a property of the equations rather than a bug
such systems amplify small differences exponentially, so any imprecision comes to dominate
the butterfly image misleads: the claim is about unknowable initial conditions, not a butterfly causing a storm
the limit is a predictability horizon of roughly two weeks
forecasters now run ensembles from varied starting points and treat the spread itself as information

A brief word about why the seasons happen, because the wrong explanation is extremely widespread and it survives even among graduates of good universities. The common answer is that the earth is closer to the sun in summer. This cannot be right for a reason available to anyone: the southern hemisphere has summer when the northern has winter, and both hemispheres are at the same distance. In fact the earth is slightly nearer the sun in January, during northern winter. The actual cause is axial tilt. The earth's axis leans by about twenty-three degrees, so through part of the orbit one hemisphere is angled toward the sun, receiving light at a steeper angle and for more hours each day. Both factors matter, and the change in day length matters more at high latitudes than the change in angle does.
options: Seasons are caused by the earth's axial tilt rather than its distance from the sun, as shown by the hemispheres having opposite seasons at the same distance, with both light angle and day length contributing.
Seasons occur because the earth's orbit brings it substantially closer to the sun during summer and further away during winter each year.
The speaker argues that axial tilt is only a minor factor and that orbital distance remains the principal cause of seasonal temperature change.
Both hemispheres experience summer simultaneously because the earth's distance from the sun changes over the course of the year.

listening.transcript: A practical word about reading difficult material, since several of you have said the theory papers are impenetrable. They are, on a first pass, and the mistake is to treat that as a failure of comprehension requiring you to slow down. Slowing down on a first reading of a hard paper is usually wasted effort, because you do not yet know which paragraphs matter. Read it quickly and badly, all the way through, accepting that most of it will not land. Then read it again knowing where it is going, and the second reading is a completely different experience because you can tell which sentences are load-bearing. Most people do the opposite: they read the first three pages four times and never reach the argument, and then conclude that the paper was too hard for them.
listening.q: What does the speaker recommend for reading difficult papers?
options: Read quickly all the way through first, then reread knowing where the argument goes.
Read slowly and carefully from the beginning until each paragraph is understood.
Read only the introduction and conclusion of difficult papers.
Discuss the paper with others before attempting to read it.

listening.transcript: A curious feature of very large organisations is that information reaching the top has been filtered at every level it passed through, and the filtering is rarely deliberate. Each layer summarises, and a summary necessarily omits, and what gets omitted is disproportionately what the person summarising expects will be unwelcome. By the time it arrives, the picture is not false so much as systematically [BEEP].

listening.spoken: Naked mole rats live in colonies organised more like those of insects than of mammals, with a single breeding female and workers that never reproduce. They tolerate oxygen levels that would kill any other mammal within minutes, switching to a metabolism fuelled by fructose when air runs short in a blocked tunnel. They are also almost entirely resistant to cancer and individuals have lived beyond thirty years roughly ten times what a rodent of that size would predict.

The deepest point in the ocean lies almost eleven kilometres below the surface, which is greater than the height of the highest mountain above sea level. Fewer people have reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench than have walked on the moon. The pressure there exceeds a thousand times that at the surface, yet the sediment supports abundant microbial life and several species of amphipod, one of which builds a protective tube from grains of the surrounding mud.
